topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; digital competency frameworks may have regional variations, and applicability to other sectors (e.g. private organisations) would require adaptation.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your public health workforce (e.g. data literacy, digital tool proficiency, cybersecurity awareness) and assess current capability gaps systematically.
Use the competency framework to structure targeted upskilling programs that move beyond ad-hoc training—ensure competencies are mapped to specific roles and career progression pathways.

Consider how digital competency requirements may differ across your organisation's hierarchy and departments; tailor development initiatives accordingly rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on public health systems in EU countries; findings on digital literacy gaps may not fully transfer to other sectors or non-EU healthcare systems, though frameworks used could have broader applicability.
takeaways: Use evidence gap analysis to identify where digital literacy interventions are most needed in your organisation — this approach helps prioritise training investments by mapping existing research against actual capability gaps.
Consider adopting or adapting the two frameworks mentioned to assess digital literacy maturity in your own public health or healthcare context before designing capability-building programs.
The focus on 'gaps' suggests that digital literacy assessments should benchmark current state against evidence-based competency models rather than relying on assumed needs.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity without full text, but likely focuses on educational framework design rather than empirical testing. Findings may not generalise beyond middle school contexts or may be geographically specific depending on curriculum standards referenced.
takeaways: AI literacy for younger audiences requires embedding AI competencies within existing digital literacy frameworks rather than teaching AI in isolation — consider how your organisation's upskilling programmes might integrate AI concepts into broader digital competency development.

Middle school-level frameworks can inform adult learning design by identifying foundational AI concepts (e.g. algorithmic thinking, bias recognition) that may be missing from your workforce's existing digital literacy baseline.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on public health faculty development; findings may not transfer directly to other sectors or non-academic organisational settings without adaptation.
takeaways: Faculty development programs can shift staff from AI resistance to readiness; design training that addresses concerns and builds confidence rather than simply introducing technical skills.
Public health organisations should invest in structured, dedicated faculty development pathways for AI literacy rather than ad-hoc workshops, as this addresses both mindset and capability gaps.

Identify and engage AI-sceptical staff early through inclusive program design; resistance often stems from unclear relevance or fear of job displacement, both addressable through thoughtful training architecture.

articles.title: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: High — systematic review methodology synthesises evidence across multiple studies and geographies, though specific labour market contexts and credential systems may vary by country.
takeaways: Data literacy is increasingly recognised as a foundational workplace skill; organisations should assess current capability gaps and prioritise structured training programs that go beyond basic spreadsheet skills to include statistical reasoning and data interpretation.

Employers need to clarify which data literacy competencies matter most for different roles rather than applying one-size-fits-all approaches — align training content with job-specific data tasks and decision-making requirements.
Data literacy gaps persist across demographic groups and education levels; targeted upskilling interventions may help reduce inequities in labour market access and advancement opportunities.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; applicability to workplace AI literacy development in non-academic settings requires contextual translation.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your learners (e.g., technical skills vs. ethical reasoning vs. prompt engineering) rather than treating AI literacy as monolithic — different roles need different depths.

Consider embedding AI literacy across existing curricula and professional development pathways rather than siloing it in standalone courses, as this improves retention and relevance to participants' actual work.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When humans and agents form a collective: a framework for collective intelligence in persistent organizational human-AI teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a theoretical framework for human-AI team dynamics, but generalisability depends on whether the framework has been empirically validated across different organisational contexts, sectors, and team sizes. No indication of field testing scope provided in snippet.
takeaways: Use the collective intelligence framework to assess your current human-AI team composition — identify whether roles, responsibilities, and decision-making authority are clearly defined between human and AI contributors to maximise synergy.

Structure persistent human-AI teams with explicit norms for information sharing, feedback loops, and escalation procedures, since collective intelligence emerges from how the group coordinates, not just individual capabilities.

Evaluate how your team balances AI automation with human oversight — collective intelligence requires clarity on when AI acts autonomously, when humans override, and when decisions are genuinely collaborative to avoid either over-reliance or underutilisation of AI.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings from nurses may not generalise to other professions or sectors; healthcare context is distinct from broader organisational settings. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools to your team, prioritise protecting and enhancing work autonomy — staff who retain meaningful control over how they use AI report better wellbeing outcomes than those who experience AI as constraining their decision-making.

AI readiness training alone is insufficient; design implementation approaches that let employees shape their own AI workflows rather than imposing standardised AI use, since autonomy is the key mechanism linking readiness to positive wellbeing.

Monitor wellbeing closely during AI transitions in your organisation, especially among healthcare or clinical staff, as the relationship between AI adoption and worker wellbeing depends critically on how much say employees have in the process.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from title and snippet alone — full text review needed to determine sample size, geographic scope, sectors included, and methodology.
takeaways: AI adoption can both enhance and inhibit employee creativity depending on implementation context — understand whether your organisation's approach supports creative autonomy or creates dependency on AI outputs.
Design AI tools and processes that preserve employee agency in creative work rather than replacing human judgment, to capitalise on creativity benefits while mitigating negative effects.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study methodology and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet alone; recommend reviewing full article for geographic scope, sector coverage, and sample size to assess applicability to Australian workplace contexts.
takeaways: AI implementation in work systems creates dual pathways affecting wellbeing — some effects are depleting (strain) while others are enriching (resources); organisations should assess which dominates in their context and intervene on the strain side.

Design AI-enabled systems with explicit attention to employee wellbeing outcomes, not just productivity; consider how automation affects workload, autonomy, skill development, and social connection rather than deploying technology in isolation.

Monitor wellbeing indicators during and after AI adoption; competing pathways suggest outcomes vary across roles and individuals, requiring ongoing measurement to identify who benefits and who experiences strain.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not provided. The conceptual framework around role ambiguity and self-efficacy in AI collaboration may apply broadly to knowledge workers, but limitations depend on the actual study population and methodology.
takeaways: Role ambiguity about how AI tools should be used is a key barrier to effective employee-AI collaboration — clarifying expectations about which tasks AI should handle and how employees should interact with it can improve adoption and outcomes.

Self-efficacy (confidence in one's ability to work effectively with AI) predicts willingness to use generative AI — invest in targeted training and early wins to build employee confidence rather than assuming adoption will follow from tool availability alone.

Address both the clarity of role expectations and individual confidence simultaneously — tackling only one pathway may leave adoption stalled if employees know how to use AI but lack confidence, or feel confident but are uncertain about appropriate use cases.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be limited by the focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in certain cultural settings (e.g., East Asian organisations). Generalisability to Western organisations with different leadership paradigms should be tested before broad application.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customising and configuring systems to their workflows—this sense of ownership increases willingness to collaborate with AI rather than resist it.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, encourage 'AI crafting' (employee-driven modifications and adaptations of AI systems) as a mechanism to build both ownership and effective human-AI collaboration.

Leaders should recognise that psychological ownership and AI crafting may operate differently across leadership styles and cultural contexts; tailor implementation strategies accordingly rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — geographic scope and sector are not identified. Generalisability depends on whether the study is single-country or multi-country, and whether findings hold across different industry types.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams working with AI tools — employees with higher psychological capital are more likely to use AI as a developmental resource rather than a threat, enabling innovation rather than passive compliance.

Create conditions where AI is framed as a job resource (a support tool that expands capability) rather than a threat — this reframing, paired with investment in psychological capital, can shift employee behaviour from defensive to generative.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective likely based on client work across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details, methodologies, and evidence base not outlined in snippet.
takeaways: Shift focus from 'AI adoption' (tool implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (behaviour change) — this requires deliberately designing human capability building, not just technology rollout.

Behaviour change for AI requires a structured change approach; identify which employee mindsets, skills, and ways of working need to shift first, then design interventions to support those specific shifts rather than generic 'AI training'.

Plan for adaptation as an ongoing process, not a one-time event — map stakeholder groups, their current capabilities, and phased milestones for building comfort and competence with AI tools over time.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but findings are not peer-reviewed and may reflect clients with greater AI adoption capacity.
takeaways: Structure AI capability building in three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) rather than attempting simultaneous transformation — this sequential approach helps organisations manage change resistance and resource constraints.

Identify and address the specific barriers at each horizon: early adoption requires building foundational skills and infrastructure; scaling requires process redesign and governance; sustained impact requires cultural embedding and continuous learning cycles.

Use the three-horizon framework to set realistic timelines and milestones for stakeholder communication, helping teams understand that meaningful organisational transformation from AI typically requires 2–3 years of sustained effort.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be an editorial or overview piece from a US business school; lacks specific empirical data or research methodology to support broad claims about AI's workplace impact.
takeaways: Identify which specific work tasks and roles in your organisation are most vulnerable to AI disruption, then proactively design reskilling or transition pathways for affected employees before change occurs.

Frame AI adoption as a collaborative tool-augmentation story rather than job replacement to reduce resistance; this narrative shift can improve employee buy-in and reduce psychological reactance to change initiatives.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The theoretical framework (cognitive appraisal of stress and Job Demands-Resources model) is broadly applicable, but the specific findings may be limited by the geographic scope and sector focus of the original study.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger job crafting through two distinct pathways — stress-based appraisal and resource-based appraisal — meaning different employees may reshape their roles in response to AI depending on how they interpret the threat or opportunity.

Managers can encourage adaptive job crafting by helping employees reframe AI awareness positively (as resources and opportunities) rather than allowing it to be interpreted primarily as a stressor, potentially improving engagement and reducing resistance.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in certain cultural settings (e.g. East Asia); findings may not transfer to Western hierarchical structures or organisations without paternalistic management styles.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customising and shaping how AI is integrated into their workflows — this sense of ownership increases willingness to collaborate with AI systems.

In paternalistic leadership environments, leverage the leader's mentoring role to guide employees toward AI crafting activities (adapting AI tools to their specific needs), which bridges the gap between ownership and actual AI adoption.

Recognise that employee-AI collaboration is not purely a technical adoption problem; it's a psychological one — ownership and crafting autonomy may be more powerful motivators than training or policy mandates alone.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven science news format without access to underlying study details, methodology, or sample characteristics. The 'shocking difference' framing suggests selective reporting and may oversimplify neuroscientific findings.
takeaways: Brain imaging continues to reveal structural and functional differences between individuals with psychopathic traits and the general population — a fascinating reminder that personality variation has measurable biological roots.

The 'shocking' framing is typical of science communication; the actual findings are likely more nuanced than headlines suggest, showing why reading the primary research matters even for fun facts about human neurobiology.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report summarising research findings without details on study sample, methodology, or geographic scope.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissists (self-centred, combative personalities) paradoxically attract romantic partners, possibly because traits like dominance and confidence read as attractiveness despite causing conflict.

The finding challenges the intuition that empathy and agreeableness are prerequisites for romantic success — some narcissistic traits can work in the short term, even if relationships may be unstable long-term.

This highlights a mismatch between what makes someone attractive initially and what makes relationships actually work — a reminder that initial chemistry and relationship quality are quite different things.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident from title alone. Frontiers publishes globally, but specific study details needed to assess generalisability.
takeaways: People with different personality traits remember surprising or unexpected events differently — some personality types may encode shock-inducing moments more vividly than others.
This reveals why eyewitness accounts of the same surprising event can vary dramatically between people; personality isn't just about how we behave, it shapes what we actually retain in memory.
A counterintuitive take on 'memorable moments' — what sticks in your brain when something unexpected happens may say more about who you are than about the event itself.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Depends on sample characteristics not provided in snippet; twin studies typically have good internal validity but generalisability varies by population source and whether both twins were raised together.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs appear to have a genetic component — suggesting personality predispositions matter as much as upbringing or political environment in shaping how people relate to authority.

Twin studies reveal nature-vs-nurture surprises: what we assume is purely learned ideology may partly reflect heritable traits like openness to experience or preference for order, making political beliefs less purely 'chosen' than we think.

This finding is counterintuitive because it challenges the idea that authoritarianism is simply indoctrination — instead pointing to biological foundations that might explain why some people are consistently drawn to hierarchical systems across different cultures and time periods.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest cross-cultural patterns in music preference and personality, though specific sample size and methodology are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Your taste in music might be a more universal personality marker than we thought — the same genres correlate with similar personality traits across different cultures and countries.
This challenges the idea that music preferences are purely culturally determined; there appear to be deep psychological patterns linking personality type to musical choice that transcend geography.
A fun conversation starter: asking someone their favourite music genre could reveal personality insights that work just as well whether they're in Melbourne, Mumbai, or Moscow.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — no information provided on sample size, geographic scope, or whether findings apply beyond wine review datasets analysed.
takeaways: Wine review language patterns can reveal personality traits — suggesting our word choices in everyday consumer contexts may leak more about who we are than we realise.
AI can spot personality signals in unstructured text data that humans might miss, opening quirky new ways to understand human expression across any domain where people write freely.
The finding connects everyday consumer behaviour (wine appreciation and description) to deeper psychology in an unexpected way — it's a fun reminder that personality shows up in mundane places.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by lack of geographic or sample details in snippet; appears to be a peer-reviewed empirical study but scope and methodology unclear without full text.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health through reduced psychological safety — leaders should proactively communicate AI implementation rationale, involve employees in rollout decisions, and create channels for voicing concerns about job security and capability gaps.

Ethical leadership is a critical buffer against depression during AI adoption — explicitly model and reinforce values around fairness, transparency, and employee wellbeing to counteract anxiety-driven by technological change.

Monitor psychological safety as a leading indicator of employee distress during AI transitions; low safety scores may predict depression and disengagement, enabling early intervention before morale and retention suffer.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample details, methodology, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Psychological safety acts as an equaliser in team dynamics, helping to reduce status hierarchies and power imbalances that can silence quieter or more junior voices — useful for designing more inclusive team structures and meeting formats.

When employees feel psychologically safe, performance gaps between different groups (e.g. by seniority, background, or role) tend to narrow, suggesting this is a lever for both equity and organisational performance.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: High — large-scale global survey across multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample composition and response rates would need verification from full report.
takeaways: Use workforce sentiment data to identify specific psychological safety gaps in your organisation — compare your team's concerns against global benchmarks to prioritise targeted interventions.
Monitor shifts in employee fears and hopes year-on-year to detect emerging trust issues early; declining psychological safety often precedes turnover and disengagement.

Share relevant findings from this global survey with leadership to build business case for psychological safety initiatives — external data can validate internal employee concerns and justify resource allocation.

articles.title: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Why Innovation Depends on Intellectual Honesty  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual arguments about innovation and intellectual honesty without empirical data or specific organisational context. Principles may apply broadly but lack evidence base for specific settings.
takeaways: Create team norms where people can voice unpopular ideas or admit uncertainty without fear of dismissal or career consequences — this directly supports both psychological safety and breakthrough innovation.
Model intellectual honesty as a leader by acknowledging what you don't know, changing your mind when presented with evidence, and rewarding team members who raise hard truths early rather than late.

articles.title: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI - Nature
articles.snippet: The work affective well-being under the impact of AI  Nature
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without full article content — snippet provides only title and journal name. Generalisability depends on study design, sample composition, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the provided information.
takeaways: Examine how AI implementation affects employee emotional experiences and job satisfaction in your organisation — this may reveal psychological safety concerns that require proactive intervention.
Monitor affective well-being (mood, engagement, anxiety) during AI adoption rollouts, as emotional responses to automation can influence team cohesion and willingness to engage with new tools.

articles.title: Fostering Ethical Conduct Through Psychological Safety - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Fostering Ethical Conduct Through Psychological Safety  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — MIT Sloan content typically draws on US-based case studies and research, though psychological safety principles are broadly applicable across organisational contexts.
takeaways: Create explicit permission for employees to raise ethical concerns without fear of retaliation or embarrassment; frame this as an organisational norm rather than an optional practice.

Link psychological safety directly to ethical outcomes in performance discussions and team rituals—teams that feel safe are more likely to speak up about misconduct, compliance issues, or process failures before they escalate.
